n: The Lord tells Isaiah to write a strange name in large, ordinary letters on a big tablet, so everyone could read it publicly. The name is a prophecy in itself.

f.g: A large tablet or writing surface.
Ordinary, common lettering anyone could read.
“Swift is the spoil, speedy is the plunder.”

n: Isaiah calls two reliable witnesses to confirm the writing, so that when the prophecy came true no one could say it was written afterward.
Isaiah’s wife, called “the prophetess,” gives birth to a son, and God tells Isaiah to give him that same name.

f.g: Isaiah’s wife — possibly a prophetess herself, or so called as a prophet’s wife.

n: Before the baby can say “Daddy” or “Mommy,” Assyria will plunder Damascus and Samaria. Damascus fell in 732 BC, and much of northern Israel was stripped soon after.
The Lord speaks to Isaiah again.
The people have rejected the gentle, quiet waters of Shiloah — Jerusalem’s small water channel, a picture of God’s quiet care — and instead delight in the two invading kings.

f.g: A gently flowing channel feeding Jerusalem’s pool (later Siloam, John 9:7).

n: So instead of a gentle stream, God will bring the mighty flood of “the river” — the Euphrates, meaning Assyria — overflowing all its banks.

f.g: The Euphrates, the great river of Mesopotamia.

n: The Assyrian flood will sweep through Judah up to the neck — nearly drowning it, but not quite. Its outspread wings cover the land of Immanuel, reminding that God is still with His people.

f.g: Assyria nearly took Judah but stopped at Jerusalem (Isaiah 36–37).

n: Isaiah taunts the nations: band together and arm yourselves if you like — you will still be shattered. The triple repetition makes it certain.
Make your plans, give your orders; they will fail, “for God is with us” — which in Hebrew is “Immanuel.”
The Lord gripped Isaiah firmly and warned him not to follow the fearful ways of the people around him.
Don’t call everything a conspiracy as the frightened people do, and don’t share their panic.
Instead, treat the Lord as holy. He alone should be the one you reverence and fear — not kings or armies.

f.w: Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself

n: To those who trust Him, the Lord will be a sanctuary. To those who reject Him, He will be a stone they trip over. The New Testament applies this to Jesus Christ.
Many will trip on that stone and fall, be broken, and be caught.
Isaiah is told to tie up and seal his testimony and teaching among his disciples, preserving it for a later time when it will be needed.

f.w: Bind up the testimony, seal the law

n: Isaiah will wait patiently for the Lord and hope in Him, even while God seems to hide His face from Israel.
Isaiah and his children, with their symbolic names, are living signs from God to Israel. Hebrews applies this verse to Christ and His followers.

f.w: I and the children whom the LORD hath given me

n: When people urge you to consult mediums and fortune-tellers who whisper and mutter, ask: shouldn’t a people seek their God? Why ask the dead about the living? 2 Nephi 18:19 reads “for the living to hear from the dead?”

f.g: Spirits of the dead supposedly contacted by mediums (Leviticus 19:31).

f.w: for the living to the dead?

n: Turn to God’s law and testimony. Anyone whose words don’t agree with them has no light — no truth or dawn — in them.

f.w: To the law and to the testimony

n: Those who reject God will wander the land distressed and starving. In anger they will curse their king and their God, looking up for help that does not come.
Looking down at the earth, they will see only trouble and gloom and be thrust into darkness. Chapter 9 answers this darkness with a great light.
